title: Grellin Power: retiring Marsh Creek
prompt: A utility sells two different things and is paid for both. The first is energy — the megawatt-hours customers actually consume, measured over a year. The second is firm capacity: a promise to the system operator that a stated number of megawatts can be delivered on demand, including on the coldest evening of the year when the sun is down. A plant that generates a great deal of energy may provide very little firm capacity, and any shortfall has to be bought from someone else in the capacity market. Our client is Grellin Power, a regional utility whose largest plant, the coal-fired Marsh Creek station, faces two changes at once: air-quality rules that require a major retrofit to keep operating, and a carbon price starting next year. Grellin has publicly pledged to cut its generation emissions by at least 60%, and its board must choose between retrofitting Marsh Creek and retiring it, replacing the output with a solar-and-storage build plus purchases from the market. They have asked us which path costs less over the next five years, and what the choice turns on.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — What Grellin has to replace if Marsh Creek closes
exhibits.text: Two obligations, not one. Energy: 5,000 GWh a year of generation that customers consume. Firm capacity: 800 MW that the system operator requires Grellin to have available on demand. Marsh Creek supplies both today. Any firm capacity Grellin cannot supply itself must be bought in the capacity market, priced per kilowatt of capacity per year.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — Marsh Creek and the retrofit (Scenario 1)

rows: Retrofit cost, one-off, to meet the air-quality rules

exhibits.unitsNote: 1 GWh = 1,000 MWh. Marsh Creek must keep delivering 5,000 GWh a year and 800 MW of firm capacity in either path.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — The replacement package

rows: Solar and storage build cost, one-off
Energy delivered by solar and storage
Firm capacity provided by solar and storage

exhibits.unitsNote: Solar and storage are credited at their de-rated contribution, not their nameplate rating: 250 MW of the 800 MW obligation. 1 MW = 1,000 kW.
exhibits.source: Grellin development team and the system operator's capacity auction results

exhibits.title: Exhibit 4 — Scenario 2: the carbon price is set at $10

rows: Retrofit cost, one-off, to meet the air-quality rules

exhibits.unitsNote: Changed from Scenario 1: the carbon price is legislated at $10 per tCO2, not $20. Every other figure, and the whole replacement package, is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Let's start with the right structure. What are the three key questions you would need to answer in order to tell Grellin's board which path to take? Please summarise them in 3 lines maximum.

keyPoints: What does each path cost in full over the horizon — capital, running cost, carbon, and anything the path forces Grellin to buy from someone else?
Does each path actually deliver what Grellin is obliged to deliver: the energy, the firm capacity, and the 60% emissions pledge?
What are the risks of each path — construction and delivery risk, exposure to market and carbon prices, and the plant's workforce and community?
commonMistakes: A generic cost-benefit framework rather than the three questions this choice turns on.
Comparing the two paths on energy alone, when the obligation has two parts.
Treating the emissions pledge as a footnote when it may be a hard constraint that decides the case.
Naming six things when the interviewer asked for three.

questions.followUp: Good. Here is what the planning team has on each path. Note that the replacement package is credited with only part of Marsh Creek's firm capacity — solar and storage are de-rated for the hours when they cannot deliver.

questions.prompt: Scenario 1: given the data in the exhibits, what is the total five-year cost of the replacement path — everything Grellin would have to pay to retire Marsh Creek and still meet its obligations? Please give your answer in $M, rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in $ millions, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Energy, per year: solar and storage 3,000 GWh = 3,000,000 MWh × $10 = $30M; market purchases 2,000 GWh = 2,000,000 MWh × $50 = $100M. Energy cost = $130M a year.
Firm capacity, per year: Grellin must hold 800 MW and the replacement package provides 250 MW, so it must buy 550 MW. 550 MW = 550,000 kW × $60 = $33M a year.
Annual cost = $130M + $33M = $163M.
Five years = 5 × $163M = $815M, plus the $1,200M build = $2,015M.
For comparison, the retrofit path is $2,050M, so the replacement is cheaper — but by $35M, not by the $200M an energy-only comparison suggests.
keyPoints: The replacement has to buy back the firm capacity that solar and storage do not provide.
Capacity is priced per kW-year, so 550 MW is 550,000 kW — a units trap worth $33M a year.
$33M a year over five years is $165M, which is most of the replacement path's apparent advantage.
commonMistakes: Costing energy only and answering $1,850M — the answer this case is designed to catch.
Multiplying 550 by $60 and adding $33,000, forgetting that the capacity price is per kW and the shortfall is in MW.
Charging the capacity shortfall against the full 800 MW rather than the 550 MW gap, and answering $2,090M.
Leaving the $1,200M build out of a 'total five-year cost'.

questions.prompt: Please explain briefly the reasoning behind your answer to the previous question, in 3 lines maximum.

keyPoints: Two obligations: the energy Marsh Creek generates and the firm capacity it guarantees, and the replacement package covers the first in full but only part of the second.
Energy costs $130M a year — solar output at its own operating cost plus the balance bought from the market.
The 550 MW of firm capacity the package does not provide has to be bought at $60 per kW-year, which is $33M a year.
Five years of that annual cost plus the one-off build gives the total, and the capacity charge is what makes the two paths close rather than far apart.
commonMistakes: Explaining the energy arithmetic without mentioning capacity at all.
Describing the capacity charge as a penalty rather than as the price of a product Grellin is obliged to hold.
Not saying how the total compares with the retrofit path.

questions.followUp: Understood. The system operator has confirmed the 800 MW obligation applies whichever path Grellin takes, and that the capacity price is set annually at auction.

questions.prompt: I'd like to check a couple of the parameters behind that. How much would Grellin pay each year in the capacity market under the replacement path? Please give your answer in $M, rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in $ millions per year, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Obligation 800 MW, provided by solar and storage 250 MW, so the shortfall is 550 MW.
550 MW = 550,000 kW.
550,000 × $60 = $33,000,000 = $33M a year.
keyPoints: Only the shortfall is bought, not the whole obligation.
Watch the units: the price is per kW-year, the shortfall is in MW.
commonMistakes: Answering $48M by buying the full 800 MW.
Answering $0.033M by treating the price as per MW.
Using the solar farm's nameplate rating instead of its de-rated 250 MW contribution.

questions.followUp: Thanks. The capacity auction has cleared between $55 and $65 per kW-year in each of the last four auctions, so $60 is a fair central figure.

questions.prompt: And what is the total five-year cost of the retrofit path — keeping Marsh Creek running? Please give your answer in $M, rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in $ millions, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Fuel and operating cost: 5,000 GWh = 5,000,000 MWh × $40 = $200M a year.
Emissions: 5,000,000 MWh × 0.9 = 4.5 Mt of CO2 a year, at $20 = $90M a year.
Annual cost = $290M.
Five years = $1,450M, plus the $600M retrofit = $2,050M.
Marsh Creek already provides the 800 MW of firm capacity, so this path buys none.
keyPoints: The carbon price is a cash cost from next year and belongs in the comparison.
The retrofit path needs no capacity purchase, which is the advantage that nearly closes the gap.
commonMistakes: Leaving the carbon cost out and answering $1,600M.
Forgetting the one-off retrofit and answering $1,450M.
Adding a capacity charge to this path, when Marsh Creek supplies the capacity itself.

questions.followUp: So the two paths are much closer than they first appear. Before the board sees this, they want to know how robust the replacement figure is.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements, if true, would change the five-year cost of the replacement path that you calculated? Select all that apply.
options: The solar and storage build would earn a production incentive of $5 per MWh on everything it generates
Grellin could contract firm capacity from a neighbouring region at $45 per kW-year instead of buying it at the auction price
The retrofit would extend Marsh Creek's life by fifteen years, far beyond the five-year window being compared
Closing Marsh Creek would trigger redundancy packages for its workforce costing $40M in total
Solar and storage are credited with 250 MW of firm capacity against Marsh Creek's 800 MW

optionRationale: Changes it. 3,000 GWh is 3,000,000 MWh, so the incentive is worth $15M a year and $75M over five years, taking the replacement path to $1,940M.
Changes it. The 550 MW shortfall at $45 rather than $60 costs $24.75M a year instead of $33M — $41.25M less over five years.

Does not change the number, and it is the strongest wrong answer here. It is a real and serious objection to comparing two paths over five years when one of them buys fifteen — but it is an argument about the horizon, not a cost inside the replacement path. Raise it with the board; do not put it in this figure.
Changes it. A one-off $40M lands on the replacement path only, since the retrofit path keeps the plant and its people.
Does not change it. That is the exhibit restated, and it is already the basis of the $33M a year you calculated.
keyPoints: Test each statement against the terms of your own calculation: energy cost, capacity cost, one-off cost.
A cost that lands on only one path still belongs in the comparison, and redundancy is exactly that.
An objection to the comparison's horizon is a real objection, but it is not a line in the cost.
commonMistakes: Picking the fifteen-year life because it is obviously important — it is, but not to this number.
Missing the redundancy cost because the case has been about megawatts rather than people.
Treating the capacity contract as a change to the obligation rather than to its price.

questions.followUp: Noted. The energy ministry has now published the legislation, and the carbon price has been set lower than Grellin's planning assumption.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is likely to be true for Scenario 2 compared with Scenario 1? Use the data below for your revised calculation. The change is described under the exhibit.
options: The replacement path is still cheaper, but by less
The retrofit path is now the cheaper of the two
The two paths now cost the same
There is not enough information to decide

optionRationale: Wrong. At $10 the carbon cost halves to $45M a year, which is a $225M swing over five years — far more than the $35M the replacement path was ahead by.

Correct. Retrofit: $200M of fuel and operating cost plus 4.5 Mt at $10 = $45M, so $245M a year, $1,225M over five years, plus the $600M retrofit = $1,825M. The replacement path is unchanged at $2,015M. The retrofit is now $190M cheaper, and the whole comparison has turned on a policy figure neither path controls.
Wrong. They are $190M apart, which is about 10% — close by the standards of a utility investment, but not the same.
Wrong. The exhibit changes one input and leaves the rest; everything the calculation needs is on the page. Worth choosing where a figure is genuinely missing, and this is not that case.
keyPoints: Break-even is a carbon price of about $18.44 per tonne: below that the retrofit wins on cost.
Grellin's planning assumption of $20 sat barely above the break-even point, which is a fragile place for a $2B decision.
Cost is not the only test: the retrofit misses the 60% emissions pledge, which the replacement path meets with an 80% reduction.
commonMistakes: Re-running the replacement path as well, when nothing in it has changed.
Halving the whole retrofit cost rather than only its carbon component.
Concluding the board should therefore retrofit, without weighing the pledge the company has made publicly.

questions.prompt: Please explain in 2 to 3 lines the reasoning behind your answer to the previous question — and say what you would now tell the board about the emissions pledge.

keyPoints: Only the carbon cost moved, and it moved by $45M a year, which over five years is far larger than the $35M gap between the paths.
So the cheaper path is now the retrofit, and the decision has been decided by a policy price rather than by anything Grellin does.
But the retrofit leaves emissions unchanged while the replacement cuts them by 80%, comfortably past the 60% pledge — so the board is now choosing between $190M and a public commitment.

A strong answer says the pledge should be treated as a constraint or priced explicitly: at $190M over five years, meeting it costs Grellin roughly $10 per tonne avoided, which is worth stating plainly.
commonMistakes: Reporting the new number without noticing that the decision now conflicts with the pledge.
Treating the pledge as automatically decisive without saying what honouring it costs.
Explaining what changed in the exhibit rather than why it changes the ranking.

questions.followUp: That is the trade the board has to make. They have also asked how to express the comparison in a way the pledge can be judged against.

questions.prompt: Choose the four pieces of data that, when combined, would allow us to estimate the cost per tonne of CO2 avoided by choosing the replacement path over the retrofit.
options: The whole-life cost of each path
The number of years over which the two paths are compared
The share of the solar farm's output curtailed at midday

optionRationale: Needed. The numerator is the extra cost of the cleaner path, which is the difference between the two whole-life costs.
Needed. The denominator starts with what the coal plant emits.
Needed, and often forgotten: the replacement path is not zero-carbon, because 2,000 GWh a year still comes from the market.
Needed. Both the cost difference and the tonnes avoided accumulate over the horizon, so the number of years scales the answer.

Not needed, and it is the tempting one. The carbon price is what you compare the answer with — if avoidance costs less per tonne than the carbon price, the cleaner path pays for itself. A benchmark is not an input.
Not needed. Curtailment would change how much energy the solar farm delivers, and that is already inside the 3,000 GWh figure and therefore inside each path's cost.
Not needed as a separate input. The capacity charge is already one of the costs inside the whole-life cost of the replacement path; taking it again would count it twice.
keyPoints: Cost per tonne avoided = (cost of the cleaner path − cost of the dirtier path) ÷ (tonnes emitted by the dirtier path − tonnes emitted by the cleaner path), over the same number of years.
That expression consumes exactly the four selected items and nothing else.
A figure you compare the answer with is not an input to it.
commonMistakes: Taking the carbon price, because a question about carbon must surely need it.
Assuming the replacement path emits nothing, and dropping its emissions from the set.
Taking the capacity price, which is already inside the path costs.

questions.followUp: Thanks. One last thing before the board paper is finished.

questions.prompt: Your BCG project leader has asked you for the risks of the replacement path — the things that could go wrong even if the arithmetic holds. Could you share your thoughts in 3 to 4 lines?

keyPoints: Delivery risk: the solar and storage build arriving late or over budget while Marsh Creek has already committed to closing, leaving Grellin buying energy and capacity at spot prices.
Price exposure: 2,000 GWh a year bought at a market price that floats, and a capacity shortfall repriced at every auction — the replacement path swaps a known fuel cost for two market exposures.
Policy risk in both directions: the carbon price has already moved once, and the capacity de-rating rules for storage could be revised.
Workforce and community: Marsh Creek's people and the town around it, and the reputational cost of handling that badly while claiming a climate win.
Physical risk: a run of poor solar years, or storage degrading faster than the de-rating assumes.
commonMistakes: Listing generic project risks with no reference to how this utility actually earns and spends.
Missing the capacity and market-price exposures, which are the two the arithmetic just introduced.
Repeating the carbon-price argument from the previous questions instead of naming new risks.

closing: That is everything. You separated the two things Grellin is obliged to deliver, priced the capacity that solar and storage do not provide, and then watched a policy price neither path controls reverse the ranking. Thank you — the board meets on Friday.
